clue.text: Doctor told lab nothing will come from it

indicators.note: to doctor something is to tamper with it, so the letters get rearranged

parts.note: anagram fodder, 7 letters

explanation.surface: A physician is told the lab work will turn up nothing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Doctor' sits at the front looking like the subject of the sentence, but it is the instruction. A dot ball is cricket: a delivery off which no runs are scored, marked as a dot in the scorebook.
explanation.definitionFit: A dot ball yields nothing: no runs come from that delivery.

clue.text: Want to accommodate Charlie round town, OK?

indicators.note: the word takes Charlie in as a guest
turning something round writes it backwards

parts.note: want = need
C in the NATO alphabet, set inside NEED to make NECED, then turned round
t = town, a map abbreviation

explanation.surface: Someone asks whether a town is fine with putting up a visitor called Charlie.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Round' belongs with the want-and-Charlie unit before TOWN is added, not with 'town'.
explanation.definitionFit: Decent and OK both mean acceptable, good enough.

clue.text: What often awaits you at A&E? Visit with no parking taking a very long time

definitions.text: What often awaits you at A&E?

indicators.note: the word has to go without the letter named

parts.note: TRIP (a visit) without P (parking)
an age = a very long time

explanation.surface: A grumble about hospital emergency visits that take forever with nowhere to park.
explanation.walkthrough: A&E (Accident and Emergency) is the British name for a hospital emergency room. The question mark flags the definition as a description rather than a synonym.
explanation.definitionFit: Triage is the sorting of patients by urgency that meets you on arrival at an emergency department.

clue.text: Reverses, so doing showing hesitation

definitions.meaning: the verb: changes direction completely, as a soldier on parade does
'so doing' means doing what the answer describes; the result is a hesitation noise, ER

explanation.surface: Someone backtracking and dithering at the same time.
explanation.walkthrough: The second half is a cryptic reading of the answer itself: ABOUT TURNS read as an instruction. Take 'about' as RE, turn it, and you get ER, the noise of someone hesitating.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym from the parade ground: to reverse direction is to turn about, and a U-turn in policy is called the same.

clue.text: 'Stick with it!' Fail occasionally getting upset

indicators.note: only now and then, so every other letter
upset in a down clue tips the letters upside down, reading them bottom to top

parts.note: the even letters of wItH iT
the even letters of fAiL, continuing the same run

explanation.surface: An exhortation to persevere, from someone who fails now and then and gets upset about it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stick with it!' reads as one phrase, but only 'Stick' is the definition; 'with it' is fodder for the alternate letters. A lathi is a heavy bamboo stick used by Indian police.
explanation.definitionFit: A loanword from Hindi: the long iron-bound bamboo club carried by police in South Asia is simply a stick.

clue.text: Corporate body running risk over start of enquiry — revealing these?

indicators.note: running as in operating: the letters are set going in new order

parts.note: the Post Office, a corporate body
anagram fodder
first letter of enquiry, placed after RISK before the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: An organisation taking risks just as an inquiry begins, and what the inquiry might expose.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface hints at the Post Office Horizon scandal and its public inquiry. Porkies is Cockney rhyming slang: pork pies = lies.
explanation.definitionFit: 'These' points back at what an enquiry into a corporate body might reveal: porkies, lies.

clue.text: Following bad feeling second intervenes quickly

parts.note: post = after, as in post-war

indicators.note: to intervene is to come between

parts.note: hate = bad feeling
s = second, inserted into HATE to make HASTE

explanation.surface: After an argument, a second person steps in fast.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Following' opens the clue and looks like a connective, but it supplies POST.
explanation.definitionFit: From old letters marked 'haste, post, haste' for the fastest courier, it became a plain synonym for quickly.

clue.text: Train flier

definitions.meaning: the railway, as in going somewhere by train
a bird: the corncrake is one of this marsh family

explanation.surface: A train that flies, or a flier on a train.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Train flier' reads as one fast express, but it is two separate definitions.
explanation.definitionFit: Rail is the train system, and a rail is also a bird.

clue.text: Why I went to Pizza Express for a starter?

definitions.text: Why I went to Pizza Express
definitions.meaning: a cryptic reading: the diner's reason for walking into a restaurant, said as four short words
a starter as a person, a beginner, not a first course

explanation.surface: A diner asking why they went to Pizza Express just for a starter.
explanation.walkthrough: Pizza Express is a British restaurant chain. The question it answers is not about the food: split the answer as IN IT I ATE. 'Starter' misleads towards the first course; here it means a beginner.
explanation.definitionFit: An initiate is a newcomer just admitted to something, so a starter in the sense of beginner.

clue.text: Grating a lot of cheese, cry after mishap

indicators.note: most but not all of the word, so its last letter goes
after a mishap the letters are in a mess

parts.note: CHEESE without its last letter
anagram fodder

explanation.surface: Someone grates too much cheese and yells after an accident with the grater.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Grating' looks like the kitchen action on the cheese, but it is the definition, meaning harsh on the ear.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: a grating voice is harsh and shrill, the quality of a screech.

clue.text: Punch's old material

parts.note: to chin someone is to punch them on the chin; the ’s reads as 'has' and joins
o = old, as in OT

explanation.surface: A question about the fabric of Mr Punch's old costume.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Punch’s' suggests the puppet of Punch and Judy, but it is a verb in disguise.
explanation.definitionFit: Chino is a twilled cotton cloth, the fabric of chinos.

clue.text: Dummy trial for Trump rejected witness

indicators.note: one thing stands in for another
sent back, so the letters are written in reverse

parts.note: the American word for a baby's dummy
trial = test, which replaces PAC
to trump = to cap (outdo); CAP written backwards is PAC, removed from PACIFIER

explanation.surface: A mock trial staged for Donald Trump throws out a witness.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Trump' is not the president but the verb to outdo, which is CAP. A dummy is British for the rubber teat given to a baby, which Americans call a pacifier.
explanation.definitionFit: A testifier is someone who gives evidence, a witness.

clue.text: Easy to pick up, Sir said previously (one's not very bright)

indicators.note: spoken, so what matters is the sound

parts.note: a knight is addressed as Sir; KNIGHT sounds like NIGHT
light = not heavy, easy to lift

explanation.surface: A teacher's aside about a pupil who is quick to learn yet not very bright.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Previously' puts the Sir part first although it comes second in the clue. 'Not very bright' sounds like a dig at a person; it is literal, a dim lamp.
explanation.definitionFit: A night-light is a dim lamp left on overnight, so one not very bright.

clue.text: Point to neat gin — it's wrong drink for test

parts.note: W = west, a compass point

indicators.note: the letters are in the wrong order

parts.note: anagram fodder, 10 letters

explanation.surface: Someone points out that neat gin is the wrong thing to drink before an exam.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer runs on into 28 across. 'Test' suggests an exam, but the test here is of the wine.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by description: the event is a drinking session whose purpose is to judge the wines.

clue.text: Promises to provide funding for archaeologist's work upfront — that's great

indicators.note: these pieces go at the front, before the promises

parts.note: pro = for, in favour of
an excavation
IOUs are written promises to pay

explanation.surface: Someone thrilled at pledges of money for an archaeological dig paid in advance.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Upfront' reads as money paid in advance; it moves PRO and DIG ahead of the IOUS.
explanation.definitionFit: Prodigious means enormous or remarkable, great.

clue.text: Preceding score no more than satisfactory

parts.note: up to = before, preceding
to score a surface is to scratch it

explanation.surface: A verdict on a result that was only passable.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Score' sounds like a result or twenty; here it is the verb to mark a surface.
explanation.definitionFit: Up to scratch means meeting the required standard and no more.

clue.text: 'So, about young woman on the internet?' (Think she may be getting suspicious)

indicators.note: about in its sense of around, so the outer word goes round the inner one

parts.note: so = thus; it goes around the young woman
e- for online plus MISS, a young woman

explanation.surface: A husband wonders whether his wife suspects his online chats with a young woman.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is the 'she' of the parenthesis: the wife whose suspicion the surface fears. The rest of the bracket fills in the picture.
explanation.definitionFit: The missus is a colloquial term for one's wife, the 'she' who may be growing suspicious.

clue.text: Caught in Scotland, maybe the biggest city in the country

definitions.text: the biggest city in the country

parts.note: a land of auks, the seabirds of Scottish cliffs; C goes inside AUK
c = caught, the cricket scorebook abbreviation

explanation.surface: A tip that the country's biggest city could be in Scotland.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The country' has no name in the clue, so it floats: Auckland is New Zealand's biggest city. 'Maybe' marks Scotland as an example of an auk land, not a definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Auckland is the largest city in New Zealand.

clue.text: Prevents originally one motelier having sex

indicators.note: take the original, first letter

parts.note: first letter of one
Norman Bates, who runs the motel in Psycho
sex is Latin for six, VI in Roman numerals; it goes inside BATES

explanation.surface: A motel owner prevents something from happening in one of his rooms.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sex' is Latin for six, not the act the motel surface suggests.
explanation.definitionFit: To obviate something is to prevent it or make it unnecessary.

clue.text: Timeless Punjabi superstar being fanciful? It won't be true

indicators.note: less means without, and time is T, so the phrase that follows drops a T

parts.note: TURBAN, the headwear of a Sikh Punjabi star, without T (time)
a legend = a superstar
flags that 'turban legend' is a whimsical description, not a real phrase

explanation.surface: A celebrated Punjabi star whose fame may be exaggerated.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags 'turban legend' as a playful description of a Sikh Punjabi celebrity, not a real phrase.
explanation.definitionFit: An urban legend is a widely told story that is not true.

clue.text: Threatened horny individual, one bothering a girl

parts.note: a = one

indicators.note: a bothered thing is disturbed, so the letters are stirred

parts.note: anagram fodder

explanation.surface: A randy man, menacing and pestering a girl.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Horny' is literal, as in having horns, and 'threatened' means endangered. The argali is a wild mountain sheep of Central Asia with huge curled horns.
explanation.definitionFit: The argali is a near-threatened wild sheep with enormous horns.

clue.text: Pop up in bookies' enclosure?

parts.note: SP = starting price, the bookmakers' odds when a race begins
the ring is the bookmakers' area at a racecourse

explanation.surface: Someone appearing suddenly in the betting area at the races.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pop up' reads as appear, and spring up is the sense.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: things that appear suddenly are said to spring up, and a jack-in-the-box both pops and springs.

clue.text: Come together shouting 'Booby!'

indicators.note: a word shouted is heard, not seen

parts.note: a booby is a fool, a nit

explanation.surface: A crowd rallying while yelling insults.
explanation.walkthrough: Nit is British slang for a fool. 'Come together' is the way broken bones knit.
explanation.definitionFit: Broken bones knit, coming together as they heal.

clue.text: Pricing rod for 'guidance' — it may be used for beating

definitions.text: it may be used for beating

indicators.note: the letters are guided into a new arrangement

parts.note: anagram fodder, 10 letters

explanation.surface: A pointer used to set prices, with a hint that it could also be used to hit someone.
explanation.walkthrough: The quotation marks around 'guidance' hint that the rearranging is its real job. A riding crop is a short whip for a horse.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by use: a jockey's short whip exists to strike the horse, and the surface's pointer hints the same.

clue.text: Not the done thing to sleep through it

parts.note: it, taken as it is
a nap = a short sleep, placed inside IT

explanation.surface: Etiquette advice: snoozing through something is bad manners.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue reads as one plain sentence about manners, and the answer describes that very thing.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: something inappropriate or unsuitable to the occasion is not the done thing.

clue.text: Content to clear Zulu fighters

indicators.note: the content of a word is its inside, without the outer letters

parts.note: LIMPID (clear) without its outer letters

explanation.surface: Zulu warriors happy to clear out.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Content' reads as happy; it is the inside of the next word's synonym. An impi is a Zulu regiment.
explanation.definitionFit: A Zulu word for an armed regiment, so a specialist term that names the fighters themselves.

clue.text: Herb Alpert releasing record — aim is to get hit

indicators.note: letting go of the letters of the record
the letters take a beating and land in a new order

parts.note: ALPERT without LP (a long-playing record)
anagram fodder

explanation.surface: The trumpeter Herb Alpert putting out a record meant to be a hit.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Herb Alpert' reads as the bandleader's full name, but 'Herb' is the definition. A 'hit' record sounds like success; here hit means knocked about.
explanation.definitionFit: Artemisia is a genus of aromatic herbs including wormwood and tarragon.

clue.text: Arab returning very soon

indicators.note: coming back, so read backwards

parts.note: in a mo(ment) = very soon

explanation.surface: An Arab coming back shortly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Returning very soon' reads as one phrase about the Arab's travel plans; 'returning' is the instruction and 'very soon' the fodder. Mo is short for moment.
explanation.definitionFit: An Omani is a person from Oman, an Arab country.

clue.text: Badmouth teacher getting sack

parts.note: to dis = to insult
pupils address a female teacher as Miss

explanation.surface: A teacher fired for speaking ill of someone.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface is a tidy story of cause and effect, so the answer seems to be in it.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: sack is informal for firing someone from a job.

clue.text: See 12
